<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" />{{rh|CHA. XXVII.|ACCORDING TO S. MATTHEW.|83 HOLY weeke.}}</noinclude>rich man of Arimathaea, named Ioseph, vvho also him self was disciple to {{sc|Iesvs}}. {{verse|chapter=27|verse=58}}† He went to Pilate, and asked the body of {{sc|Iesvs}}. Then Pilate commaunded that the body should be deliuered. {{verse|chapter=27|verse=59}}† {{MarginNote|margin=right|margin-width=65|text={{sc|Hora completorii}}, or Complin.}}And Ioseph taking the body, {{sup|‖}} vvrapt it in cleane sindon, {{verse|chapter=27|verse=60}}† and laid it in his ovvne nevve monument, vvhich he had hevved out in a rocke. And he rolled a great stone to the doore of the monument, and vvent his vvay. {{verse|chapter=27|verse=61}}† And there was there Marie Magdalene, and the other Marie, sitting ouer against the sepulchre.

{{verse|chapter=27|verse=62}}† {{MarginNote|margin=right|margin-width=65|text={{sc|Satvrday}} called Sabbatum sanctum.}}And the next day, vvhich is after the Parasceue, the cheefe Priestes and the Pharisees came together to Pilate, {{verse|chapter=27|verse=63}}† saying, Sir, we haue remembred, that that seducer said yet liuing, After three dayes I vvil rise againe. {{verse|chapter=27|verse=64}}† Commaund therfore the sepulchre to be kept vntil the third day: lest perhaps his Disciples come, and steale him, and say to the people, He is risen from the dead: and the last errour shal be vvorse then the first. {{verse|chapter=27|verse=65}}† Pilate said to them, You haue a gard: goe, gard it as you knovv. {{verse|chapter=27|verse=66}}† And they departing, made the sepulchre sure: sealing vp the stone, vvith vvatchmen.

{{c|{{larger|A N N O T A T I O N S}}}}
{{c|{{sc|Chap. XXVII.}}}}

''3. Repenting him.''] {{MarginNote|margin=right|margin-width=65|text=Horrour of conscience.}}Note how spedily the plague of God falleth after sinne, and specially men must note what torment of conscience, and desperation often foloweth the sheading of innocent bloud.

''5. Hung him self.''] {{MarginNote|margin=right|margin-width=65|text=Desperation.}}If he had rightly repented, notwithstanding his horrible treason, he might haue obteyned mercy: but by hanging him self he tooke away al meanes of mercy and saluation, because he died finally impenitent.

''24. Innocent of his bloud.''] {{MarginNote|margin=right|margin-width=65|text=They that execute lawes against their cōscience, are like to Pilate.}}Though Pilate was much more innocent then the Iewes, and would haue been free from the murder of our Sauiour, seeking al the meanes that he could (without offending the people and the Emperours lawes) to dimisse him: Yet he is damned for being the minister of the peoples wicked wil against his owne conscience. euen as al Officers be, and specially the Iudges and Iuries which execute lawes of temporal Princes against Catholike men: for al such be guilty of innocent bloud, and be nothing excused by that they execute other mens will according to the lawes, which be vniust. For they should rather suffer death them selues, then put an innocent man to death.

''40. If thou be the Sonne.''] {{MarginNote|margin=right|margin-width=65|text=Christ derided in the B. Sacrament, euen as vpō the Crosse.}}Maruel not, when thou hearest our Sauiour in the B. Sacrament mocked at, or seest him abused of wicked men, that he straight reuengeth not such blasphemies: or that he sheweth not him self there visibly and to the senses, when faithles Heretikes wil say, Let me see him, tast him, &c. for he suffered here the like on the Crosse, when he might at his will haue come downe with as much ease as he rose when he was dead.

''46. Why hast thou forsaken me.''] Beware here of the detestable blasphemie of Caluin and the Caluinists, {{MarginNote|margin=left|margin-width=65|text=''Catechis. Calu. & Instit. li. 2 16''.}}who thinking not the bodily death of Christ sufficient, say, that he was also here so forsaken and abandoned of his Father, that he sustained in soule and conscience the very feares and torments of the damned. ''And'' to take away the Article of his descending into Hel after his death, (which was {{MarginNote|margin=right|margin-width=65|text=Caluins blasphemie.}}with triumph and not in paine,) ''they'' say that his descending was nothing els, but that his soule suffered the very paines of Hel vpon the Crosse. Whereas in deede by these wordes out of the Psalme, our Sauiour wil signifie no more but that his paines (being now so long on the Crosse and ready to die) were very great, and therfore according to the infirmity of his humane nature, for very anguish (as before in the garden when he was but toward his Passion) he saith he<noinclude>{{rh||L ij|was}}</noinclude>
